Future Heist: Turn an electoral opening into public pressure

The opportunity

Tuesday’s election created an opening to challenge Big Oil’s influence in Texas. Democrats defeated all eight statewide Republicans, despite receiving $423,000 in oil and gas contributions to the Republicans’ $34.7 million—an 82-to-one advantage, according to Future Heist’s analysis.

The Texas House also appears on track to flip.

But an electoral victory is not automatically a climate victory.

Full results and sources are at futureheist.org/texas-oil-money-2026.

Two fights converge as the legislature opens January 12 and fracking wastewater discharge permits move through TCEQ. The industry needs new disposal routes to expand: in August, industry representatives told a Texas Senate committee that growth depends on permission to discharge wastewater into rivers and spread it on farmland. We will help affected communities challenge those routes and press the new legislature for stronger protections.

We don’t need to lead with climate to win on climate. We can win by making the industry’s flood of waste into the focus of the fight.

What we will do

Future Heist has identified 57,726 landowners potentially affected by waste facilities and proposed wastewater discharges. Our initial priorities are 2,249 owners with a registered waste pit on their land and 60 who own land next to proposed discharge sites. The remaining owners have land within two miles of an oilfield waste dump with a pending permit.

Their opposition can help block projects, put pressure on legislators and build support for stronger waste-disposal rules.

By January 12, we will:

  1. Reach landowners. Send letters to the 2,309 priority owners, take their calls and follow up with respondents. With Earthjustice, prepare the first hearing request before TCEQ issues its first draft permit.

  2. Connect participants with partners. Help owners document their experiences and connect potential permit challengers with Earthjustice. Work with Commission Shift and Texas Permian Future Generations on state legislative outreach, and Fieldnotes on federal outreach.

  3. Support legislation and coverage. Supply research and constituent stories for Commission Shift’s wastewater bills, give reporters hearing materials and fact sheets, and build a shared tracker of bills partners support and oppose.

We will support, not replace, partners’ legal and organizing work. A hearing itself depends on partner participation and the regulatory timetable.

A record to build on

Since February, Future Heist has published or supported 15 stories in major publications, with 82 pickups across 70 outlets. These include our own work in MS NOW, HEATED and the Texas Observer, and reporting based on our research in the Houston Chronicle and Texas Tribune. We also turn state records into public tools, including a map ranking every Texas oil and gas well by its risk of failure.

The immediate ask: a ten-week sprint to January 12

Bill filing begins Monday. We are seeking ten weeks of bridge funding, through January 12, at one of two levels.

$62,000 launches the base program: Saul and Greg’s research, outreach and communications work, including letters to the 2,309 priority owners. Follow-up will depend on their capacity; this level does not fund dedicated organizers. The base program costs $312,000 for 2027.

$230,000 launches the expanded program: outreach to all 57,726 landowners, staff to follow up with respondents, and organizers at Commission Shift and Texas Permian Future Generations, paid through those organizations directly. Contributions above the base budget will expand this work.

About $1.1 million funds the expanded program from now through the end of 2027, including an outreach hire, an engineer to build data and outreach tools, and a full year of partner organizing staff.
